analysis.title: The macro is breaking so why are stocks refusing to
key_insights: DXY has held its major trendline in place since 2011 and reclaimed its 200-week moving average. The technical setup resembles late 2021.

MUFG reports a record $1.47 trillion of foreign purchases of US equities and corporate bonds in the year to August, almost double the pre-GFC peak. FX hedge ratios are still low, so the inflows are a strong source of dollar demand.
SocGen's Albert Edwards says excess liquidity has deteriorated sharply. Historically it has been a good leading indicator for equities, though the relationship is imperfect.

Edwards also flags that breadth of analyst earnings revisions has deteriorated, especially in tech, and the change in the pace of upgrades has rolled over. Equities can struggle without earnings falling if the good news stops accelerating.

BofA says off-balance-sheet AI commitments rose more than 50% between quarters, while traditional debt and lease liabilities rose more modestly. Including Nvidia's newly disclosed obligations, the combined total is approaching $3.5 trillion. Not all of it is debt and some can be cancelled.

GS tech specialist Jim Callahan asks what happens to the AI ecosystem without Jensen Huang as CEO. Nvidia has supported neoclouds and others through investments, commercial commitments and supplier ties, and a new CEO may be less willing to use the balance sheet that way. Near-term chip demand may not change, but the longer-term financing model could.
Hartnett (BofA) says the global tightening cycle is far from over, with more than 70 rate hikes expected between June 2026 and May 2027. The April FOMC is the earliest potential turning point.
BofA notes the surging dollar and gold below $4,000 signal retreating global liquidity. Sticky CPI leaves little room for lower Treasury yields to support risk assets, even with oil down 15%.

Cyclicals are weak: lumber -21%, metals -11%, blue-collar semis -26%. Consensus still expects 5-6% nominal GDP growth and more than 15% EPS growth in 2027, so the next revision looks more likely to be down.
Volatility has retreated from Thursday's panic extremes but remains elevated, particularly in tech. The equity bounce has not calmed the options market.
Forward P/E and PEG ratios are near their 35-year averages (Datastream). That does not make equities cheap given concentration, but it weakens the blanket bubble argument.
Seasonality is supportive into year-end, and the setup follows a violent positioning reset. Lighter positioning and seasonal demand may be enough for a rally without better fundamentals.

GS buyback desk estimates S&P 500 buyback demand at about $5bn per day, with 90% of companies in their open repurchase window by Monday. Volumes picked up in the back half of the week, and the demand could support a year-end squeeze.
earnings_insights: Earnings are still growing at a healthy pace, but SocGen's Edwards says revision breadth has deteriorated, particularly in tech, and the rate of change in upgrades has rolled over.
Hartnett notes consensus still expects more than 15% EPS growth in 2027 and says the next revision looks more likely to be down.

risk_factors: Dollar strength continuing to tighten global liquidity.
Excess liquidity deteriorating, which has historically led equities lower.
Earnings revision momentum rolling over, particularly in tech.
Growing off-balance-sheet AI commitments approaching $3.5 trillion combined.
Dependence of the AI ecosystem on Nvidia's balance sheet if Jensen Huang leaves as CEO.
Global rate hikes and sticky CPI limiting any relief from lower yields.
Consensus nominal GDP and 2027 EPS growth estimates too high.
Elevated tech volatility in the options market.
